Cut these: the life story, the adjective pile, the mumbled ask, the 45-second monologue. Write your 4 parts, cut to 30 seconds, swap an adjective for a number, practise this week. www.internwise.co.uk

captionThread: An interview is a two-way read. Most candidates only play one side. Here's how to spot the buying signals and the red flags. A thread.

Green flags they want you: they shift from testing you to selling the role, they ask what you'd want in year two, the 30-min slot runs to 45, they pull in a colleague mid-interview.

captionThread: Every 'tell me about a time...' question is asking for the same thing: a clear story in a clear shape. STAR is that shape. A thread on how to use it without sounding robotic.

Without structure: 'Well, so basically in second year, before that I did this thing, and there was a project, kind of...' With STAR: four sentences, clear beginning, clear end. Interviewers score you higher on communication.
S = Situation. One sentence. Where, when, what team. Skip the backstory of the backstory. 15 seconds of context is enough.
T = Task. What YOU needed to do. Make your role obvious, not the team's. This is where interviewers separate you from the group.
A = Action. 60% of your answer lives here. Use 'I' not 'we'. Every sentence. Show judgment, not just activity.
R = Result. Numbers, always numbers. Even rough estimates land. Tie it back to the task. End with what you learned - shows self-awareness.
3 stories every grad needs ready: a time you led something, a time you handled conflict, a time you failed and learned. Drill them into STAR shape. Find interviews at www.internwise.co.uk

posts.title: Iced Coffee Stirs Job Interview Debate
posts.caption:
A Guardian article picked up a debate that started online: is it unprofessional to arrive at a job interview holding an iced coffee?

The real story is not the drink. It is how small signals get judged in interviews, especially when the candidate is early in their career. Some hiring managers may read a takeaway cup as too casual. Others may see that reaction as outdated, because it says little about whether someone can actually do the job.

For students and graduates, the useful lesson is this: interviews still come with unwritten rules. You do not need to become robotic, but you do need to think about the first impression you are creating before the first question is asked.

Practical takeaway: keep the focus on your preparation, examples, and fit for the role. If something might distract the interviewer before you have made your case, leave it outside the room.

Source: The Guardian.

posts.title: New Plan May Raise Training Costs for Older Workers
posts.caption:
The UK government plans to overhaul apprenticeship funding. This proposal would make employers pay more to train older workers than younger apprentices. The aim is to tackle youth unemployment by incentivising companies to hire more young people. 

For students and recent graduates, this means more opportunities could open up as businesses may look to take on younger apprentices. It's a move to help combat youth joblessness and create pathways into the workforce.

Internships are a crucial way to gain experience and make yourself attractive to potential employers. They help bridge the gap between education and a full-time job, equipping you with practical skills.

Source: The Guardian.
